Protect sensitive fields during document preparation and application requests, then control what each authorized user can see.

01

Why protect RAG data

RAG brings enterprise knowledge into the model context. Data protection determines which sensitive values travel with it.

Retrieval-augmented generation combines an LLM with information retrieved from external sources. Relevant passages, account information or service responses are supplied with a user request so the model can produce a more grounded answer. This can improve freshness and relevance without retraining the model. Google Cloud explains this retrieval and grounding pattern.

The same flow can expose customer names, contact details, financial information, health records, credentials and confidential business content. Exposure can occur during document conversion, embedding, retrieval, prompt assembly, model processing, response handling or logging.

The Thales examples apply protection at two points: before documents are made available to downstream AI systems, and before user prompts and retrieved context reach a generative model. Policy-controlled reveal can then govern what an authorized user sees.

RAG and training are different operations

RAG supplies information at request time; it does not itself train or fine-tune the model. The ETL output can also support a separately designed training workflow, but neither example demonstrates model training on protected data.

02

One design across two data flows

Data preparation

Protect the knowledge source

Discover sensitive documents, convert supported formats, inspect the extracted content and apply CipherTrust protection before a downstream loader indexes or uses it.

Application requests

Protect the model context

Authenticate the caller, collect user and business context, protect detected sensitive fields and send the resulting context to the model.

CipherTrust Manager supplies the keys and protection policies used by the data protection components. CipherTrust Secrets Management (CSM) supplies application secrets and referenced configuration. Imperva WAF and API Security can protect the exposed application boundary as an additional deployment layer.

03

What each layer contributes

LayerPurposeHow it fits
Discovery and classificationFind candidate data sourcesThales Data Discovery and Classification (DDC) exports a report used by the ingestion example.
Sensitive data inspectionFind sensitive values in textGoogle Cloud DLP inspection identifies the configured information types. Detection quality depends on coverage, likelihood thresholds and document extraction.
CipherTrust data protectionProtect field valuesThe web application uses CipherTrust REST Data Protection (CRDP). The local batch example currently uses CipherTrust Application Data Protection (CADP), with a REST alternative in source.
Policy-based revealControl presentation of protected dataThe trusted application supplies the authorized identity to the reveal service; policy can permit cleartext, masking or another configured result.
Secrets managementKeep service credentials outside application sourceThe web backend resolves CSM secret references at startup. Bootstrap credentials still require secure delivery and restricted access.
WAF and API SecurityProtect public endpointsImperva can inspect traffic, apply API controls and reduce exposure to common web attacks. Configure routing, TLS and origin restrictions for the deployment.
04

What the user sees

A user asks a question containing a name or email address. The backend combines it with business context, inspects the combined text and replaces detected sensitive values with protected representations. Non-sensitive context remains readable so the model can still answer the business question.

Illustrative input

Summarize the support issue for Alex Morgan and contact alex.morgan@example.com.

Illustrative model context

Summarize the support issue for [protected person] and contact [protected email].

These placeholders explain the concept. The example code uses policy tags and length-delimited protected values rather than these literal labels.

For an approved user, a reveal operation can return the representation allowed by policy. Another user may receive masked data. The application must establish identity and authorization before it requests a reveal; a name typed into a form is suitable for a demonstration, but is not an authorization control.

The supplied UI also includes a sensitive-output simulator. It lets a demonstrator enter sample content, protect it and show a policy-controlled result alongside the LLM answer. This illustrates output handling without claiming that a public model was trained on the sample sensitive data.

05

How the design addresses AI risks

The following mappings use the OWASP 2025 risk categories. Data protection contributes to a broader set of controls.

RiskContribution of this designComplementary controls
LLM02 Sensitive Information DisclosureReduce cleartext sensitive values in prompts, retrieved context and downstream data.Inspect all relevant sources, minimize data, restrict access and keep raw content out of logs.
LLM05 Improper Output HandlingUse protection and authorized reveal as part of response handling.Validate outputs, encode for the destination and constrain downstream actions.
LLM03 Supply ChainUse managed secrets to reduce credential exposure.Review dependencies, verify artifacts and manage vulnerabilities. Secrets storage alone does not secure the supply chain.
LLM08 Vector and Embedding WeaknessesProtect documents before embedding and preserve access metadata.Enforce tenant and document access during retrieval and evaluate index leakage and retrieval quality.

Protection of sensitive fields does not stop prompt injection or establish that retrieved content is trustworthy. Retrieval authorization, source provenance, output validation and safe tool use remain separate requirements.

06

Design decisions that matter

Protect before embedding

Embedding is another model call. Apply the ingestion protection boundary before content reaches an embedding service. Access restrictions are still needed for vectors and stored chunks.

Preserve retrieval usefulness

Semantic search over protected identifiers may behave differently. Keep useful non-sensitive context and evaluate relevance using representative questions and policy settings.

Coordinate protection policies

Exact matching across ingestion and query paths requires compatible policies, keys, normalization and deterministic behavior where supported. A shared tag format alone does not make values match.

Keep cleartext within its boundary

The trusted preparation and application services still handle raw values, and DLP receives content for inspection. Protect staging files, service connections, logs and access to those systems.

Decide how much the model needs to know

Protected fields can reduce disclosure while preserving surrounding meaning, but they can also limit tasks that need the original values. Measure detection coverage, answer quality, retrieval quality and authorized reveal behavior together.

07

A practical path to adoption

  1. Select a bounded use case. Identify the source documents, sensitive fields, users and expected answers.
  2. Define policies and identities. Decide which fields to protect and which users may see cleartext, masked data or no data.
  3. Prepare the knowledge source. Run discovery, conversion and protection, then validate output before indexing.
  4. Connect the application. Protect the full prompt context and implement response inspection and authorized reveal.
  5. Validate the boundaries. Test missed detections, unauthorized access, dependency failures, retrieval relevance and model output handling.

Build the two flows

The companion implementation guide maps the design to Java classes, configuration, API examples and the ETL commands.
